name: Kris Yao
bio:
Kris Yao (born 1951) is a Taiwanese architect, founder and head of KRIS YAO | ARTECH, with offices in Taipei and Shanghai. Born and raised in Taipei, he studied at Tunghai University and took a master's degree at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1978, then set up his firm in 1985. Its work, mostly in Greater China, ranges from stations for Taiwan High Speed Rail, such as Hsinchu, to the Southern Branch of the National Palace Museum in Chiayi and the Wuzhen Theater in China. He received Taiwan's National Award for Arts in 2007.

The Lanyang Museum in Yilan (2010) takes its form from the tilted rock ridges, or cuestas, of the Beiguan coast: its roof rises from the ground at 20 degrees to meet a wall at 70. Water-Moon Monastery (Nung Chan Monastery) in Taipei (2012), a Buddhist monastery he rebuilt that year, won the Taiwan Architecture Award in 2013. The China Steel Corporation Headquarters in Kaohsiung (2012), 29 storeys and 135 metres high, is four tubes bound around a central core, with a faceted façade that shifts every eight floors to make outdoor terraces.

UC Berkeley 1978; projects: THSR Hsinchu Station, Southern Branch of the National Palace Museum, Wuzhen Theater, Lanyang Museum, Water-Moon Monastery, China Steel Corporation Headquarters; Venice Biennale 2003; 2007 National Award for Arts; 2013 Taiwan Architecture Award for Water-Moon Monastery

name: Leslie Martin
bio:
Sir Leslie Martin (1908–2000) was an English architect, a leading advocate of the International Style, whose work was especially influenced by Alvar Aalto. Born in Manchester, he trained at Manchester University. After the war he joined the London County Council, became its chief architect in 1953 and used the post to promote younger architects such as James Stirling and Alison and Peter Smithson. From 1956 he headed the architecture school at Cambridge, where with Colin St John Wilson he designed Harvey Court, one of the most important examples of brick brutalism. He received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1973.

For the Royal Festival Hall in London (1951), the main building of the Festival of Britain, he led the design team under Robert Matthew; his 1948 sketch shows the concert hall as an "egg in a box", a raised auditorium wrapped in foyers. He later designed the extension to Kettle's Yard in Cambridge (1970), a gallery for works by Barbara Hepworth, Ben Nicholson and others. The Centro de Arte Moderna Gulbenkian in Lisbon (1983) was added that year to the Gulbenkian Foundation's park as its modern art centre.

name: Lev Rudnev
bio:
Lev Rudnev (1885–1956) was a Soviet architect and a leading practitioner of Stalinist architecture. Born in Novgorod, the son of a schoolteacher, he studied painting and architecture at the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg under Leon Benois and Ivan Fomin. In 1917 he designed the avant-garde Monument to the Fighters of the Revolution in Petrograd. He taught at the Academy of Arts in Leningrad from 1922 to 1948 and then at the Moscow Architectural Institute, and after the Second World War helped rebuild Voronezh, Stalingrad, Riga and Moscow.

The Government House, Baku (1952), built from 1936 after a competition he won, houses ministries of Azerbaijan and was designed for 5,500 people. The Moscow State University Main Building (1953) on the Sparrow Hills, designed with a team and awarded the Stalin Prize, is the tallest of Moscow's "Seven Sisters" and was Europe's tallest building from 1953 to 1990. In the same spirit he designed Warsaw's Palace of Culture and Science (1955), offered as a gift to the people of Poland; 237 metres high with its spire, it was dedicated to Stalin on completion.

name: Lluís Domènech i Montaner
bio:
Lluís Domènech i Montaner (1849–1923) was a Catalan architect and politician, one of the shapers of Catalan Modernisme, the local form of Art Nouveau. Born in Barcelona, he studied physics and natural sciences before switching to architecture, qualifying in 1873, and taught at and directed Barcelona's school of architecture for 45 years. His buildings mix rationalism with rich ornament drawn from Spanish-Arabic architecture. He chaired the Lliga de Catalunya and the Unió Catalanista, and left politics in 1904.

The Palau de la Música Catalana (1908), built from 1905 for the choral society Orfeó Català, uses exposed red brick and iron, mosaics, stained glass and glazed tiles to give a feeling of openness and transparency. Casa Fuster (1911), built from 1908 for Mariano Fuster at the top of the Passeig de Gràcia, was the last town house he designed and has been a hotel since 2004. The Hospital de Sant Pau (1930), built from 1901, is twelve pavilions in a large green space linked by underground galleries, the largest complex built in Art Nouveau; with the Palau it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

name: Lundgaard & Tranberg
bio:
Lundgaard & Tranberg is a Danish architecture practice in Copenhagen, founded in 1985 by Boje Lundgaard and Lene Tranberg. In the 1990s it was known mainly for heat and power plants and other technical buildings; its breakthrough with the wider public came in the mid-2000s with the Charlottehaven housing (2004) and above all with a student hall and a theatre. Lundgaard left in 2004, just as this success arrived, and Tranberg has led the practice since with a new group of partners. Its buildings have won six RIBA European Awards.

Tietgenkollegiet in Copenhagen's Ørestad (2006), the student hall, is a seven-storey ring inspired by the round Hakka houses of southern China, cut into five sections by vertical passages; every room faces outward, while kitchens, lounges and terraces face the central courtyard to bring residents together. The Royal Danish Playhouse (2008), the theatre, projects about 40 per cent of its bulk over the water and is edged by a 150-metre promenade of rough oak planks on crooked, Venetian-style columns. Kannikegården in Ribe (2015), beside the cathedral, followed.

name: Marcello Piacentini
bio:
Marcello Piacentini (1881–1960) was an Italian architect and urban theorist, one of the main proponents of Italian Fascist architecture. Born in Rome, the son of the architect Pio Piacentini, he began with picturesque housing inspired by Italian vernacular building, and in 1912 took charge of Italian building works in Cyrenaica, in Libya. Under Mussolini he became the regime's favoured agent for rebuilding central Rome: his 1931 plan led to the Via dell'Impero and the clearing of the area around the Mausoleum of Augustus, and he designed the new campus of the Sapienza University (1932) and the EUR district, where Mussolini made him High Commissioner.

The Palazzo di Giustizia, Milan (1940), the city's courthouse, was built from 1932. For the industrialist Ermelino Matarazzo he designed the Matarazzo Building (São Paulo City Hall) (1939), a headquarters for his companies with an Art Deco look, now the city hall of São Paulo. After the war he won few prestigious commissions; among them was the Palazzo dello Sport at EUR (1960), designed with Pier Luigi Nervi from 1958, which hosted the basketball tournament of the 1960 Olympics.

name: Mario Roberto Álvarez
bio:
Mario Roberto Álvarez (1913–2011) was an Argentine architect whose office, MRA, designed public buildings, offices, hotels and towers across Buenos Aires. Born in the city, he graduated from the University of Buenos Aires in 1936 with a gold medal and in 1938 won a scholarship to study and work in Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. Back home he became director of architecture for the suburb of Avellaneda in 1942 and founded MRA with Leonardo Kopiloff and Eduardo Santoro in 1947. Later works include the Le Parc tower (1996), the tallest in Argentina until 2003, and the Hilton Buenos Aires (1999). In 2007 the city named him an Illustrious Citizen.

The firm's first major commission, won in 1954, was the Teatro General San Martín on Corrientes Avenue (1960), the largest centre for the stage in Argentina. Its success brought the adjoining Centro Cultural General San Martín (1973), built from 1962. For the state steel company he designed the SOMISA Building in Buenos Aires (1977), its headquarters, in the same years as the Hernandarias Subfluvial Tunnel and the Salto Grande Dam.

name: Masato Otaka
bio:
Masato Otaka (1923–2010) was a Japanese architect and urban planner and a founding member of the Metabolist group. He graduated in architecture from the University of Tokyo in 1947 and joined Kunio Maekawa's office in 1949, where as a junior associate he completed the Harumi Apartment Building in Tokyo Bay. Around the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo he formed the Metabolist group with Kisho Kurokawa, Kiyonori Kikutake, Fumihiko Maki and others, and with Maki wrote its essay "Towards the Group Form". He opened his own office in 1962 and worked largely as a planner, including the master plan for Tama New Town (1966).

Sakaide Artificial Ground (1968) lays a new ground like a slab over the old, crowded district of salt-marsh workers in Sakaide: instead of clearing the city, Otaka built a layer on top of it, a form of urban growth by superimposition tied to his idea of "collective forms". The Gunma Prefectural Museum of History in Takasaki (1979), designed by his office, won the BCS Prize. The Fukushima Prefectural Museum of Art (1984), also by his office, stands at the foot of Mount Shinobu.

name: Maxwell Fry
bio:
Maxwell Fry (1899–1987) was an English modernist architect, writer and painter. Born in Liscard, Cheshire, he trained at Liverpool's school of architecture in the neo-Georgian classicism of Charles Reilly, then turned to modernism and became closely involved in the MARS Group, the English branch of CIAM; he practised with Walter Gropius, Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret. From the 1940s he and his wife, the architect Jane Drew, designed mainly educational buildings in Ghana and Nigeria, and in the 1950s they spent three years with Le Corbusier creating Chandigarh, the new capital of Punjab. He received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1964.

The Sun House in Hampstead (1936) is among his best-known houses of the 1930s and is listed Grade II*. Kensal House in Ladbroke Grove (1937), two curved blocks of 68 flats for the Gas Light and Coke Company, developed with the social reformer Elizabeth Denby and with a community centre, laundry and nursery school, was the first modernist block in Britain designed for working-class tenants. The Times considered the University of Ibadan (c. 1955) in Nigeria his most notable work in West Africa.

name: Mecanoo
bio:
Mecanoo is an architecture practice based in Delft, in the Netherlands, founded in 1984 by Francine Houben, Henk Döll, Roelf Steenhuis, Erick van Egeraat and Chris de Weijer. Houben, Döll and Steenhuis had won, while still students at Delft University of Technology, a competition for youth housing at Kruisplein in Rotterdam that marked a turning point in Dutch social housing. Between 1988 and 2003 four of the five founders left; Houben remains creative director. Its many libraries range from Delft University of Technology's (1997) to the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library in Washington (2020).

Montevideo in Rotterdam (2005), designed by Houben, is a 152-metre tower of flats, offices and shops, one of the tallest buildings in the world designed by a woman. The Library of Birmingham (2013) has been described as the largest public library in the United Kingdom. The National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts in Taiwan (2018), whose design Houben drew from the area's banyan grove, links four halls and an outdoor theatre through an open Banyan Plaza and is described as the world's largest performing arts centre under one roof.

name: Mohsen Foroughi
bio:
Mohsen Foroughi (1907–1983) was an Iranian architect, a founder in 1945 of the Association of Iranian Architects and the first Iranian graduate of the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where he won the prize for the best diploma in 1937. Back in Tehran he helped André Godard, Maxime Siroux and Roland Dubrulle found the university's Faculty of Fine Arts in 1940, later succeeding Godard as dean. With Heydar Ghiai he designed the Senate House in Tehran. He is best known for Niavaran Palace (1958), the Shah's residence from 1967 until the 1979 revolution.

For the National Monuments Council he designed tombs of Persian poets. The Tomb of Saadi in Shiraz (1952), built from 1950, draws on the Chehel Sotoun pavilion. The Mausoleum of Baba Taher in Hamadan (1970) gave the poet's grave its present form. In Paris he and Ghiai prepared a first design for the Fondation Avicenne (Maison de l'Iran) (1969), a student residence at the Cité internationale universitaire; when the city authorities rejected it, André Bloc brought in Claude Parent, and the four completed it together, on three welded-steel frames about 38 metres high.

name: Moisei Ginzburg
bio:
Moisei Ginzburg (1892–1946) was a Soviet architect and a leading theorist of Constructivism. Born in Minsk into a Jewish family of architects, he studied at the Milan Academy of Fine Arts and the Riga Polytechnic Institute and moved to Moscow in 1921 to teach at VKhUTEMAS. His book Style and Epoch (1924), often compared to Le Corbusier's Vers une architecture, served as a manifesto for Constructivist architecture. He founded the OSA group of Constructivist architects. After the group was dissolved in the early 1930s he turned to planning and worked mainly in Crimea and Central Asia.

The Gosstrakh Apartments in Moscow (1927) were the first building in the USSR to apply Le Corbusier's Five Points. The Narkomfin building (1930), designed in 1928 with Ignaty Milinis for staff of the People's Commissariat of Finance, was a "social condenser": a long block of duplex flats on pilotis with a roof garden, linked by a bridge to a block of shared facilities. Le Corbusier acknowledged it as an influence on his Unité d'Habitation. The Government House of the Kazakh ASSR (now KBTU) in Almaty (1931), designed in 1928, followed.

name: Ove Arup
bio:
Sir Ove Arup (1895–1988) was a British engineer, born in Newcastle to a Danish father and a Norwegian mother, the founder of the firm Arup and among the foremost structural engineers working with architects in his time. He studied philosophy and then engineering at the Technical University of Denmark and came to London in 1923 for the firm Christiani & Nielsen. In the 1930s he was structural consultant to Berthold Lubetkin's Tecton on the Penguin Pool at London Zoo and Highpoint I. During the war he helped design the Mulberry harbours for D-Day. He set up Arup and Partners in 1946 and was design engineer of the Sydney Opera House.

Kingsgate Bridge in Durham (1963), the firm's first bridge, was designed and built under his personal supervision; it was the last structure he designed, and his ashes were scattered from it. Beside it stands Dunelm House (1966), the student union completed under his supervision, a listed brutalist building. Preston Bus Station (1969), designed by Building Design Partnership, was engineered by Ove Arup & Partners, whose curved car-park balconies came about when acceptable finishes for a straight wall proved too expensive.

name: Paul Andreu
bio:
Paul Andreu (1938–2018) was a French architect and engineer, known for airports around the world and for large cultural buildings in China. Born in Gironde, he studied at the École Polytechnique and the École des Ponts, then architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts, graduating in 1968. From 1967 he led the planning and building of Charles de Gaulle Airport for Paris, and his airports range from Shanghai Pudong to Cairo. In 2004 part of his Terminal 2E at Charles de Gaulle, opened in 2003, collapsed and killed four people; an inquiry cited technical causes and a lack of safety margins in the design, while Andreu blamed poor execution by the builders.

Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport Terminal 1 (1974), the airport's first terminal, is a circular building, unlike the linear terminals that followed. The Shanghai Oriental Art Center (2005) groups five domed halls like the petals of a butterfly orchid seen from above. The National Centre for the Performing Arts in Beijing (2007), nicknamed "the boiled egg", sets its theatres inside an ellipsoidal shell of more than 18,000 titanium plates and glass, set in an artificial lake.

name: Pedro Ramírez Vázquez
bio:
Pedro Ramírez Vázquez (1919–2013) was a Mexican architect responsible for some of Mexico's most emblematic buildings, known for designs that blended European modernism with pre-Columbian forms, mostly in concrete. Persuaded into architecture by the poet Carlos Pellicer, he graduated from the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) in 1943. His system for rural schools built thousands of them and was later used by UNICEF. His National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City (1964) won the grand prize at the São Paulo Biennial. He presided over the organising committee of the 1968 Mexico City Olympics and founded the Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana.

The Museo de Arte Moderno in Chapultepec Park (1964), designed with Rafael Mijares, houses modern Mexican art. The Estadio Azteca (1966), also with Mijares, hosted the football final of the 1968 Olympics; with 87,523 seats it is the largest stadium in Latin America. The Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe (1976), designed with a team including José Luis Benlliure, replaced an older, sinking church; its circular form recalls the tent that sheltered the Ark of the Covenant, and its 10,000 seats lie under a self-supporting roof without columns.

name: Peter Behrens
bio:
Peter Behrens (1868–1940) was a German architect and graphic and industrial designer, and a pioneer of corporate design. Born in Hamburg and trained as a painter, he showed himself an architect with his own Jugendstil house at the Darmstadt Artists' Colony (1901), designed down to the towels. In 1907 he was a founding member of the German Werkbund and began working for the electrical company AEG, designing its logotype, products, publicity and buildings; for this he is considered the first industrial designer in history. Mies van der Rohe, Le Corbusier and Walter Gropius all worked in his office early in their careers.

The Hagen Crematorium (1907), built from 1905 in Hagen-Delstern, was among the early works in which he turned to simple, rectilinear volumes and classical sources. The AEG Turbine Factory in Berlin (1909), his best-known work, is a steel-framed hall about 100 metres long with 15-metre windows set between bare steel columns whose bolts and joints show; it is considered the first attempt to bring restrained modern design to industrial building. The German Embassy, Saint Petersburg (1913) was admired by Hitler, according to Albert Speer.

name: Raj Rewal
bio:
Raj Rewal (born 1934) is an Indian architect based in New Delhi. He studied in Delhi and London and worked for Michel Ecochard in Paris before opening his practice in New Delhi in 1962. His works include the National Institute of Immunology and the Parliament Library in New Delhi and the Ismaili Centre in Lisbon. He received the Indian Institute of Architects' Gold Medal in 1989, and in 2018 his drawings and models entered the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the first by an Indian architect.

The Hall of Nations in New Delhi (1972), engineered by Mahendra Raj for the Asia 72 trade fair, was the world's first space frame built in reinforced concrete and the largest in span when built; it was demolished in 2017. The Asian Games Village (1982), built for the athletes of that year's games in Delhi, arranges its housing around a hierarchy of courtyards. The State Trading Corporation Building (1989), built from 1976, joins ideas from Japanese Metabolism with Mughal tradition: its structurally expressive frame of Vierendeel trusses is clad in polychrome sandstone instead of bare concrete.

name: Ralph Erskine
bio:
Ralph Erskine (1914–2005) was a British architect and planner who lived and worked in Sweden for nearly his whole career. Born in London to socialist parents and sent to a Quaker school, he took from Quaker ideals his view of society and architecture. Shortly before the Second World War he moved to Sweden, drawn by the work of Asplund, Markelius and Lewerentz and by its welfare state. In Luleå he designed a shopping centre of 1955 described as the first purpose-built enclosed shopping centre in the world. He received the Wolf Prize in 1983 and the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 1987.

The Byker Wall in Newcastle upon Tyne (1982) is a long, unbroken block of 620 maisonettes; the architects opened an office on site to build trust with residents, though fewer than a fifth of the original residents were rehoused there. Lilla Bommen in Gothenburg (1989), an 86-metre, 22-floor office tower, is known for its red-and-white colours as "the Lipstick". The Aula Magna at Stockholm University (1997) lines its hall in blond wood under a steeply sloping ceiling shaped to spread the sound.

name: Ram Karmi
bio:
Ram Karmi (1931–2013) was an Israeli architect known for his brutalist work. Born in Jerusalem, the son of the architect Dov Karmi, he grew up in Tel Aviv, served in the 1948 war and studied at the Technion in Haifa and the Architectural Association in London. His early buildings included the Negev Center in Beersheba (1960) and the Tel Aviv Central Bus Station, long criticised as hard to find one's way in. After the Six-Day War of 1967 he rethought his brutalism, and from 1974 to 1979 he was chief architect of Israel's housing ministry, reworking its public housing. He received the Israel Prize in 2002.

He completed the Hecht Synagogue in Jerusalem in 1981. With his sister Ada Karmi-Melamede he won the 1986 competition for the Supreme Court of Israel (1992); set on a hill in Jerusalem, it joins traditional motifs with post-modern design, and Paul Goldberger wrote that in it "the sharpness of the Mediterranean architectural tradition and the dignity of the law are here married with remarkable grace." From 2007 he led the renovation of the Habima Theatre in Tel Aviv (2012).

name: Robert Matthew
bio:
Sir Robert Matthew (1906–1975) was a Scottish architect and a leading proponent of modernism. Born and raised in Edinburgh, he studied at Edinburgh College of Art and in 1945 became chief architect and planning officer of the Department of Health for Scotland. From 1946 to 1953 he held the same post at the London County Council, in charge of post-war rebuilding, housing such as the Roehampton estate, and the Festival of Britain. He then became the first professor of architecture at the University of Edinburgh and in 1956 founded RMJM with Stirrat Johnson-Marshall. He was president of the RIBA from 1962 to 1964 and received its Royal Gold Medal in 1970.

As the LCC's chief architect he led the Royal Festival Hall project in London (1951), gathering a young team in which Leslie Martin came to lead the design. Central Hall, University of York (1968), a brutalist hall designed by John Speight of RMJM, is listed Grade II. The Royal Commonwealth Pool in Edinburgh (1970), by RMJM with Ove Arup & Partners, was built for the aquatic events of the 1970 Commonwealth Games and is listed Category A.

name: Román Fresnedo Siri
bio:
Román Fresnedo Siri (1903–1975) was a Uruguayan architect best known for major civic buildings in South America and the United States. Born in Salto, he studied architecture at the University of the Republic in Montevideo from 1923 to 1930. An admirer of Frank Lloyd Wright's organic architecture, he was among the Latin American winners of the Museum of Modern Art's 1940 Organic Design competition. As chief architect of the national power company UTE he designed its headquarters in Montevideo, the Palacio de la Luz, gold medallist at the 1948 Pan American Congress of Architecture.

With Mario Muccinelli he won the 1938 competition for the Faculty of Architecture, University of the Republic (1946), in Montevideo, an early landmark of Latin American modernism declared a national historic monument in 2000. The Hipodromo do Cristal in Porto Alegre (1959), won in a 1951 international competition, is among his most notable works for its flamboyant design and engineering. The Pan American Health Organization Headquarters in Washington (1965), also won in competition, opened that September: a curved office block that echoes the Montevideo faculty, with a circular council chamber for 400 delegates.

name: Sedad Hakkı Eldem
bio:
Sedad Hakkı Eldem (1908–1988) was a Turkish architect known for seeking a national modern architecture, adapting the International Style to Turkish domestic traditions instead of applying it uniformly. Born in Istanbul, he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts and opened his own office in 1932 while teaching at the Academy until 1978. In 1934 he founded its National Architecture Seminar to record traditional Turkish houses; this work led to his books on the Turkish house, among them the five-volume Türk Evi (1984). With Emin Onat he designed the Istanbul Palace of Justice.

For the Hilton Istanbul (1955), designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, he worked with Gordon Bunshaft, adding Ottoman and Turkish elements to Bunshaft's modern lines; it is the longest-operating Hilton outside the United States. The Social Security Complex, Zeyrek (1970), designed from 1962, shows the horizontal roof lines, wide canopies and cantilevers of his late work, and won him the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1986. The Atatürk Library in Taksim (1976), a three-storey concrete building of hexagonal units, was planned as part of a cultural complex of which only the library was built.

name: Shin Takamatsu
bio:
Shin Takamatsu (born 1948) is a Japanese architect from Nima, in Shimane Prefecture, known for futuristic designs that often borrow anthropomorphic or mechanical imagery. He graduated from Kyoto University in 1971, worked for Kiyoshi Kawasaki's office and opened his own practice in 1980, the year he completed his doctorate. His early buildings in Kyoto were small, strictly symmetrical, hard-edged and machine-like, and were read as part of Japanese post-modernism: Origin I (1981) won the Japan Institute of Architects' newcomer award in 1984, and Kirin Plaza in Osaka the Architectural Institute of Japan Prize in 1989. From about 1990, as his commissions grew larger, he turned to big glass volumes instead. He taught at Kyoto University from 1997 to 2013.

Back in his home region he designed the Nima Sand Museum (1990) in Shimane and, in neighbouring Tottori, the Shoji Ueda Museum of Photography (1995), for which he received the Minister of Education's Art Encouragement Prize in 1996. The National Theatre Okinawa in Urasoe (2003) belongs to his later, larger public work, alongside the Tianjin Museum in China (2004), which he won in an international competition.

name: Teodoro González de León
bio:
Teodoro González de León (1926–2016) was a Mexican architect known for large public buildings in Mexico City. He studied at the national school of architecture of UNAM from 1942 to 1947 and, on a French government scholarship, spent 1948–49 in Le Corbusier's office. While still a student he put forward the original concept for UNAM's Ciudad Universitaria campus, now a World Heritage Site. From 1974 to 1982 he designed public buildings with Abraham Zabludovsky, among them the INFONAVIT headquarters, and later the Mexican embassy in Berlin (2001). He received Mexico's National Prize for Arts and Sciences in 1982 and the UIA Gold Medal in 2008.

El Colegio de México (1976), the main building of the college's new campus in the south of the capital, was one of his works with Zabludovsky. So was the Museo Tamayo in Chapultepec Park (1981), which houses the collection of the painter Rufino Tamayo; its design earned both architects the National Prize in 1982. The Museo Universitario Arte Contemporáneo (2008), Mexico's first public museum devoted to 21st-century art, sets a minimal, sloping glass façade against the surrounding buildings of the 1970s.

name: Tezuka Architects
bio:
Tezuka Architects is a Tokyo practice founded in 1994 by the married architects Takaharu Tezuka (born 1964) and Yui Tezuka. Takaharu studied at the Musashi Institute of Technology and the University of Pennsylvania and spent four years with the Richard Rogers Partnership in London before the two set up their office. Their buildings, many of them houses, schools and hospitals, put human activity and connection first. The practice received the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture in 2017.

The Roof House in Hadano (2001) won the Japan Institute of Architects Prize and the Yoshioka Prize in 2002. The Echigo-Matsunoyama Museum of Natural Science (Kyororo) (2003) is a 160-metre structure of weathering steel plates weighing about 2,000 tonnes, whose rust protects it from further corrosion; its name comes from the call of the ruddy kingfisher. Fuji Kindergarten in Tachikawa (2007) is an open-air school built on the idea that children need not be forced to learn: trees grow up through it for children to climb, and crates rather than walls divide the classes. In 2011 the OECD named it the best of its exemplary educational buildings.

name: UNStudio
bio:
UNStudio is a Dutch architecture practice in Amsterdam, founded in 1988 by Ben van Berkel and Caroline Bos as Van Berkel en Bos Architectenbureau. The initials stand for United Network, a reference to the collaborative, international team it draws on; it now has more than 250 staff and offices in Shanghai, Hong Kong, Frankfurt, Dubai and Melbourne. Its work runs from infrastructure to houses: early projects included the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam (1996) and the Möbius House (1998), and later ones Arnhem Centraal station (2015) and the stations of the Doha Metro.

The Galleria Department Store (West) in Seoul (2004) was given a new façade of 4,330 glass discs on its concrete skin, with a foil that gives a mother-of-pearl sheen by day and LED lights behind each disc that can be programmed at night. The Mercedes-Benz Museum in Stuttgart (2006) is built on a cloverleaf of three overlapping circles around a triangular atrium; a double-helix route fits 16,500 square metres of exhibition space onto a 4,800-square-metre footprint and lets visitors switch between two tours. The Agora Theatre in Lelystad (2007) followed.

name: Van den Broek en Bakema
bio:
Van den Broek en Bakema was a Rotterdam architecture practice that played a leading part in rebuilding the Netherlands after the Second World War. It grew from the office of Brinkman & Van der Vlugt, whose work Jo van den Broek carried on from 1936; in 1948 he brought in Jaap Bakema (1914–1981). Named Van den Broek en Bakema from 1951, the firm made its name with the Lijnbaan shopping street in Rotterdam (1953) and the plan for a city on the artificial island of Pampus (1965). Bakema was also a member of Team 10 and an editor of the magazine Forum. The office continues today as Broekbakema.

The Aula TU Delft (1966), one of the few brutalist buildings left in the Netherlands, cantilevers a 34.5-metre concrete hall for 1,040 seats on mainly two columns. Marl Town Hall (1967) sets a council wing under a 60-metre folded roof of prestressed concrete, as an open, non-authoritarian town hall. Terneuzen City Hall (1972), on the dike along the Westerschelde, recalls a great ship; Bakema put the citizens' hall on the top floor and called it "a hospitable house of chunky material".

name: Vann Molyvann
bio:
Vann Molyvann (1926–2017) was a Cambodian architect and urban planner, the pioneer of New Khmer Architecture, which joined modernism to Khmer tradition and to the country's climate and heavy rains. Born in Kampot province, he studied architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris until 1954. Back in Cambodia in 1956, he was made state architect and head of public works by Prince Norodom Sihanouk and built more than 100 structures, among them the Chaktomuk Conference Hall and the new town of Sihanoukville. He lived in exile in Switzerland through the civil war and the Khmer Rouge years, and from 1991 headed APSARA, the authority for Angkor, until his dismissal in 2001.

The Independence Monument (Cambodia) in Phnom Penh (1962), marking independence from France in 1953, is a 37-metre lotus-shaped stupa in the manner of the temple at Banteay Srei. The National Olympic Stadium (1964), designed in 1962 for 60,000 spectators and ringed by a moat against flooding, was built in under two years; he considered it his greatest achievement. His other buildings in the capital include the Institute of Foreign Languages (1972).

name: Walter Netsch
bio:
Walter Netsch (1920–2008) was an American architect based in Chicago, closely associated with brutalism and with Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. He joined SOM in 1947, became its partner for design and stayed until 1979, opening his own practice in 1981. His signature approach, Field Theory, builds complex shapes from rotating squares. He was lead designer for the United States Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs and led the team for the University of Illinois Circle Campus in Chicago. He designed 15 libraries and the east wing of the Art Institute of Chicago.

The Inland Steel Building in Chicago (1958), designed with Bruce Graham, was the first skyscraper built in the Loop after the Great Depression: 14 exterior columns carry its whole weight, leaving the offices inside free of columns. The Cadet Chapel, US Air Force Academy (1962), is a row of seventeen spires formed by a tubular steel frame of 100 identical tetrahedrons, clad in aluminium, with coloured glass filling the gaps between them. The Joseph Regenstein Library at the University of Chicago (1970) is built of grooved limestone that from a distance looks like concrete.

name: Wang Shu
bio:
Wang Shu (born 1963) is a Chinese architect based in Hangzhou who, with his wife and partner Lu Wenyu, founded Amateur Architecture Studio in 1997; the name rebukes the "professional, soulless architecture" they blame for the demolition of China's old neighbourhoods. Born in Ürümqi, he studied architecture at Southeast University in Nanjing and became dean of the School of Architecture of the China Academy of Art. In 2012 he became the first Chinese citizen to win the Pritzker Prize; the jury praised his "unique ability to evoke the past, without making direct references to history", and the award drew criticism for leaving out Lu Wenyu, who he said deserved to share it.

His buildings use traditional materials and older techniques, often with bricks and tiles salvaged from demolished buildings. The Ningbo Museum of Art (2005) was built from 2001. The Vertical Courtyard Apartments in Hangzhou (2007) were nominated for the International Highrise Award. The Ningbo History Museum (2008) has a façade built entirely of recycled bricks and a form that recalls the nearby mountains; it received the Lu Ban Prize, China's top architecture prize, in 2009.
